etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English scharp, from Old English sċearp, from Proto-West Germanic *skarp, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”).

Cognate with West Frisian skerp, Low German scharp, Dutch scherp, German scharf, Danish skarp. Compare Irish cearb (“keen; cutting”), Latin acerbus (“tart, bitter”), Tocharian B kärpye (“rough”), Latvian skârbs (“sharp, rough”), Russian щерба (ščerba, “notch”), Polish szczerba (“gap, dent, jag, chip, nick, notch”), Albanian harb (“rudeness”). More at shear.

definitions.definition: Terminating in a point or edge, especially one that can cut or pierce easily; not dull, obtuse, or rounded.

quote.citation: 1879, R[ichard] J[efferies], chapter II, in The Amateur Poacher, London: Smith, Elder, & Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Orion hit a rabbit once; but though sore wounded it got to the bury, and, struggling in, the arrow caught the side of the hole and was drawn out. Indeed, a nail filed sharp is not of much avail as an arrowhead; you must have it barbed, and that was a little beyond our skill.

quote.citation: 1984, Michael Grater, Paper Mask Making, →ISBN, page 55:
quote.text: If a knife which is sharp is incorrectly used it will obviously be dangerous.

quote.citation: 2002, Carol Pier, Tainted Harvest, →ISBN:
quote.text: Fifteen children reported handling curvos, five machetes, and one a sharp knife used to cut yellow leaves off the banana plants.

quote.citation: 2006, Werner U. Spitz, Daniel J. Spitz, Russell S. Fisher, Spitz and Fisher's Medicolegal Investigation of Death, →ISBN:
quote.text: Yet, review of 25 years of English language literature on the subject of sharp force injury adds remarkably little to this topic. Sharp force covers a vast array of injuries produced with sharp objects capable of cutting or stabbing or both.

definitions.definition: (colloquial) Intelligent.

quote.citation: 2015 February 20, Jesse Jackson, “In the Ferguson era, Malcolm X’s courage in fighting racism inspires more than ever”, in The Guardian (London)‎[1]:
quote.text: At school, despite his sharp mind, Malcolm was laughed at by teachers when he said he wanted to be a lawyer.

definitions.definition: (music) Raised by one semitone (denoted by the symbol ♯ after the name of the note).
(music) Higher in pitch than required.
Having a strong acrid or acidic taste.
Sudden, abrupt, intense, rapid.

quote.citation: 1914 November, Louis Joseph Vance, “An Outsider […]”, in Munsey’s Magazine, volume LIII, number II, New York, N.Y.: The Frank A[ndrew] Munsey Company, […], published 1915, →OCLC, chapter II (Burglary), page 378, column 1:
quote.text: She wakened in sharp panic, bewildered by the grotesquerie of some half-remembered dream in contrast with the harshness of inclement fact,  […]

definitions.definition: (colloquial) Illegal or dishonest.
(colloquial) Keenly or unduly attentive to one's own interests; shrewd, verging on dishonest.

quote.citation: 1732, Jonathan Swift, Considerations Upon Two Bills:
quote.text: But, as they have hitherto stood, a clergyman established in a competent living is not under the necessity of being so sharp, vigilant, and exacting.

definitions.definition: Exact, precise, accurate; keen.

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Catherine Clabby, “Focus on Everything”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: Not long ago, it was difficult to produce photographs of tiny creatures with every part in focus. […] A photo processing technique called focus stacking has changed that. Developed as a tool to electronically combine the sharpest bits of multiple digital images, focus stacking is a boon to biologists seeking full focus on a micron scale.

definitions.definition: Offensive, critical, or acrimonious; stern or harsh.

quote.citation: 1976 August 14, John Mitzel, Richard Hall, “The Whodunit Writer: Why He Dun It”, in Gay Community News, volume 4, number 7, page 7:
quote.text: The reviews have ranged from excellent (In Touch, Jan 76, and Gay Literature, Winter 76) to qualified praise (GCN, 6 Mar 76) to sharp attack (Allen Young in the current Gay Liberator; Allen calls it trivial and misogynist.

definitions.definition: (colloquial) Stylish, smart or attractive.

quote.citation: 2024 July 13, Laura Onita, Eleanor Olcott, “Shein's master of reinvention treads tricky path to IPO”, in FT Weekend, page 11:
quote.text: A sharp dresser partial to snakeskin shoes whose miniature Australian shepherd dog Saatchi is a constant fixture on family outings, [Donald] Tang's next move was to reinvent himself as a dealmaker connecting China with Hollywood amid growing demand for entertainment content in both countries.

definitions.definition: Observant; alert; acute.
Quick and alert.
Strongly distinguishing or differentiating; acute.
Forming a small or tight angle; especially, forming an angle of less than ninety degrees.

quote.citation: 1900, Charles W[addell] Chesnutt, chapter I, in The House Behind the Cedars, Boston, Mass.; New York, N.Y.: Houghton, Mifflin and Company […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The street down which Warwick had come intersected Front Street at a sharp angle in front of the old hotel, forming a sort of flatiron block at the junction, known as Liberty Point

definitions.definition: Steep; precipitous; abrupt.
(mathematics, of a statement) Said of as extreme a value as possible.
(chess) Tactical; risky.

quote.citation: 1963, Max Euwe, Chess Master Vs. Chess Amateur, page xviii:
quote.text: Time and time again, the amateur player has lost the opportunity to make the really best move because he felt bound to follow some chess "rule" he had learned, rather than to make the sharp move which was indicated by the position.

quote.citation: 1975, Luděk Pachman, Decisive Games in Chess History, page 64:
quote.text: In such situations most chess players choose the obvious and logical way: they go in for sharp play. However, not everyone is a natural attacking player […]

definitions.definition: Piercing; keen; severe; painful.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: Sharp misery had worn him to the bones.

quote.citation: 1785, William Cowper, The Task: The Winter Walk at Noon:
quote.text: The night was Winter in his roughest mood; the morning sharp and clear.

quote.citation: 1867, John Keble, “St. Peter's Release”, in J.G.Holland, editor, Christ and the Twelve: Scenes and Events in the Life of Our Saviour and His Apostles, page 424:
quote.text: In sharpest perils faithful proved, Let his soul love thee to the end.

definitions.definition: Eager or keen in pursuit; impatient for gratification.
(obsolete) Fierce; ardent; fiery; violent; impetuous.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, Paradise Lost:
quote.text: And fear of God, from whom their piety feign'd In sharp contest of battle found no aid Against invaders

quote.citation: 1665, John Dryden, The Indian Emperor: Act III:
quote.text: A sharp assault already is begun;

definitions.definition: Composed of hard, angular grains; gritty.

quote.citation: 1700, Edward Moxon, Mechanical Exercises:
quote.text: Well-burnt good lime and sharp sand, if very sharp, a load of sand (about 36 bushels) to a hundred of lime (being 25 bushels, or a hundred pecks […]

definitions.definition: (phonetics, dated) Uttered in a whisper, or with the breath alone; aspirated; unvoiced.
(obsolete) Hungry.

quote.citation: 1782, Frances Burney, Cecilia, II.iii.1:
quote.text: “[W]hy this last week we ha'n't had nothing at all but some dry musty red herrings; so you may think, Miss, we're kept pretty sharp!”

quote.citation: 1881–1882, Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island, London; Paris: Cassell & Company, published 14 November 1883, →OCLC:
quote.text: “ […]  It’s child’s play to find the stuff now. I’ve half a mind to dine first.”“I don’t feel sharp,” growled Morgan.

definitions.definition: To a point or edge.
Piercingly.

quote.citation: 1853, Matthew Arnold, Sohrab and Rustum:
quote.text: The iron plates rang sharp, but turn'd the spear

definitions.definition: Eagerly.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: You bite so sharp at reasons.

definitions.definition: So as to make a sharp, or tight, angle.
In a sharp manner: a less usual alternative to sharply in certain senses.
(of times of day, not comparable) Exactly.
(music) In a higher pitch than is correct or desirable.

quote.citation: 1867, Dutton Cook, Hobson's Choice, Chapter 8, “Music Hath Charms”, p. 72 [3]
quote.text: Whereas Matilda Milner frequently sang sharp, in spite of the efforts of Miss Brown, who played the accompaniment, to give her the right note and keep her in tune.

definitions.definition: (music) The symbol ♯, placed after the name of a note in the key signature or before a note on the staff to indicate that the note is to be played one chromatic semitone higher.
(music) A note that is played one chromatic semitone higher than usual; denoted by the name of the note that is followed by the symbol ♯.
(music) A note that is sharp in a particular key.
(music) The scale having a particular sharp note as its tonic.
(medicine) A hypodermic syringe.
(medicine, dated) A scalpel or other edged instrument used in surgery.
(psychiatry, healthcare) A sharp object; any item pointed enough to injure human skin.
(usually in the plural) Something that is sharp.

quote.citation: c. 1700, Jeremy Collier, On Duelling:
quote.text: If butchers had but the manners to go to sharps, gentlemen would be contented with a rubber at cuffs.

definitions.definition: A dishonest person; a cheater.

quote.citation: 1885, W[illiam] S[chwenck] Gilbert, Arthur Sullivan, composer, “A More Humane Mikado”, in  […]  The Mikado; or, The Town of Titipu, London: Chappel & Co., […], →OCLC, Act II, page 36:
quote.text: The billiard sharp whom anyone catches / His doom's extremely hard— [...]

definitions.definition: Part of a stream where the water runs very rapidly.

quote.citation: 1858, Charles Kingsley, “Chalk Stream Studies”, in Fraser's Magazine:
quote.text: here are good fish to be picked out of sharps and stop-holes into the water-tables

definitions.definition: A sewing needle with a very slender point, more pointed than a blunt or a between.
(in the plural) Fine particles of husk mixed with coarse particle of flour of cereals; middlings.

quote.citation: 1954, Barbara Comyns, Who Was Changed And Who Was Dead, Dorothy, published 2010, page 21:
quote.text: While he worked he talked to his ducks, who were waddling about hopefully, as it was almost time for the red bucket to be filled with sharps and potato-peelings.

definitions.definition: (slang, dated) An expert.
A sharpie (member of Australian gangs of the 1960s and 1970s).

quote.citation: 2006, Iain McIntyre, Tomorrow Is Today: Australia in the Psychedelic Era, 1966-1970:
quote.text: The Circle was one of the few dances the older sharps frequented; mostly they were to be found in pubs, pool-halls or at the track.

definitions.definition: Alternative form of sharpie (“type of fishing boat”)
(music) To raise the pitch of a note half a step making a natural note a sharp.

That new musician must be tone deaf: he sharped half the notes of the song!

definitions.definition: To play tricks in bargaining; to act the sharper.

quote.citation: 1692, Roger L’Estrange, “ (please specify the fable number.) (please specify the name of the fable.)”, in Fables, of Æsop and Other Eminent Mythologists: […], London:  […]  R[ichard] Sare, […], →OCLC:
